hints: Start by thinking about what carries phosphate ions up from the roots and where most of that flow ends up in a transpiring plant.
Now think about the direction of flow in xylem and whether xylem vessels actually reach into the very tips of roots and shoots.
walkthrough:
Follow the transpiration stream**
Phosphate ions absorbed by roots enter the xylem and are carried passively upwards in the mass flow of water. Because leaves have a huge surface area and many stomata, they lose most water by transpiration and so receive most of the xylem flow.

Why tips miss out**
Xylem vessels end before the meristems at root and shoot tips, and flow in xylem is essentially one-way upwards to transpiring leaves, not downwards to root tips. Leaves also have a high demand for phosphate for photosynthesis, ATP and nucleotides, so much is unloaded there.

Putting the suggestion together**
So only a small proportion reaches growing points directly through xylem. Supply to root tips and shoot apices must largely involve transfer to phloem or cell-to-cell movement, not direct xylem delivery.

Final answer: Most water in the xylem moves in the transpiration stream to the leaves, carrying dissolved phosphate ions with it; xylem does not extend into growing points / shoot and root tips and transports upwards only, so little phosphate reaches the tips directly.

hints: Look first at where the $^{32}P$ label appears in the stem below the fed leaf - compare phloem values with xylem values in both group A and group B.
Focus on what is different about group A - what does an impermeable waxed paper barrier between phloem and xylem test for?
Compare the same region and same tissue between groups, for example xylem in S1 or S2 in A versus B, to decide if movement between tissues occurs.
Pick one pair of numbers to quote as evidence and think about why percentages fall from S1 to S4 and why totals do not add to 100%.
walkthrough:
Phloem carries label down from the leaf**
In both groups the phloem in S1 to S4 below the leaf contains $^{32}P$, for example 12% in S1 phloem in A and 15% in S1 phloem in B. That tells you phosphate injected into the leaf vein has moved out of the leaf and into the stem, and downwards in phloem, which can transport in any direction from source to sink.

Xylem labelling needs an explanation**
Xylem below a leaf would not normally receive sap directly from that leaf, because xylem flow is upwards. Yet xylem in S1 to S4 contains some label, especially in group B with no barrier, for example 5% and 6% in S1 and S2 xylem. The simplest route is lateral movement from phloem to xylem in the stem.

The waxed paper proves lateral transfer**
Group A has impermeable waxed paper between xylem and phloem and shows almost no label in xylem: 1%, <1%, 0%, <1% in S1 to S4. Group B with no paper shows consistently higher xylem values: 5%, 6%, 2%, 1%. Like-with-like comparison in the same region, such as S1 xylem 1% in A versus 5% in B, supports the idea that the barrier prevented phloem to xylem movement.

Building a balanced discussion**
Also note that some label may be unloaded to surrounding stem cells, and much injected phosphate remains in the leaf or has moved elsewhere in the hour, so totals do not sum to 100%. The data do not prove upward movement in xylem, only downward movement in phloem followed by sideways transfer to xylem.

Final answer: Labelled phosphate moves out of the leaf into stem phloem and downwards; it can transfer laterally from phloem to xylem. Waxed paper prevents this transfer, so xylem labelling is much lower in group A than B, e.g. in S1 1% in xylem in A compared with 5% in B, and xylem values are higher in B in all regions S1 to S4.
